extracted.intended_audience: readers of Philosophical Transactions — natural philosophers, physicians, and surgeons (17th-century scientists and clinicians)
extracted.subtask_description: Contemporaneous scientific reports and case accounts across natural philosophy (earthquakes, astronomy, clinical cases, epidemics) intended for learned readers; includes observational claims, methodological remarks, and practical medical/surgical guidance. Extracts implicit/practical standards embedded in narrative reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earthquake-resistant building practice (Spanish houses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spaniards who inhabited this island ... built their houses very low; and they consisted only of ground-rooms, their walls being made of posts, which were as much buried under-ground as they stood above, purposely to avoid the danger which attended another manner of building, from earthquakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical recommendation observed in the field: build low single-storey ground-rooms with posts deeply set/partly buried to reduce earthquake hazard. Example: 'wary Spaniards' built low houses that fared better in violent shocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report earthquake chronology and observable sequence of shocks
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts consistently specify exact time, sequence, and character of shocks (e.g., 'between 11 and 12 o'clock at noon' ; 'it began with a small trembling ... immediately succeeded the third shock which in less than a minute's time shook the very foundation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When documenting an earthquake report include the time of occurrence, sequence (number and relative strength of shocks), short-term aftershocks (frequency per hour/day), and immediate physical sensations (ground heave, rumbling sounds). Examples in text: first small tremor, second stronger, then a violent third shock; continued shaking 5–6 times in 24 hours or multiple shocks per hour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe acute geomorphic and hydrodynamic effects precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative emphasizes effects such as ground rising like waves, sand boilling/opening and swallowing people, water spouting up and flooding streets, the sea retreating and returning, mountains falling and blocking rivers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good observational reporting records specific geomorphic phenomena (ground heave, fissuring, sand liquefaction, emergent springs), hydrodynamic events (sea withdrawal, tsunamilike inrush, rivers stopped or re-routed), and their locations/extent (e.g., 'north about 1000 acres of land sunk'). Use these details to infer mechanism and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference about spatial distribution of shaking (proximity to mountains relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a generally received opinion, that the nearer to the mountains, the greater the shake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observed spatial variation of intensity to hypothesize earthquake source or amplifying features: proximity to mountainous regions may correlate with stronger shaking in these accounts; record both mountain and coastal effects for comparative inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallax method limitations for fixed-star distances
rubrics_metrics.description: The ancient astronomers ... by their parallax to the semidiameter of the earth ... being never able to discover any in the fixed stars ... Since the Pythagorean system ... the diameter of the earth's annual course ... might give a sensible parallax to the fixed stars ... But there are some considerations which may make us suspect, that even this is not large enough for that purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological criterion: to determine stellar distances by parallax you must have a baseline large enough that the parallax angle exceeds instrument resolution. Huygens' failure to detect apparent magnitude through 100x glasses implies that parallax of fixed stars is below detectability with available telescopes. Use assumptions about stellar size (e.g., assume star similar to sun) to derive limits. The author draws concrete conclusions: (1) Earth's orbital diameter is negligible compared to star distances; (2) approaching stars by a large fraction would change apparent size only slightly; (3) most interstellar space receives little extra light from stars; (4) light travel times are enormous relative to human voyages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative assumptions about stellar physical size when inferring distances
rubrics_metrics.description: Since in all likelihood the fixed stars are suns, perhaps of different magnitudes, we may, as a reasonable medium, presume they are generally about the size of our sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When estimating distances from apparent angular size, adopt explicit assumptions about intrinsic stellar diameter; state the assumption (e.g., 'stars ~ size of Sun') and propagate it through parallax/angle reasoning to estimate minimal distances and to evaluate detectability given instrument magnification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical guidance for epidemic 'general cold' (encourage sweating; avoid bleeding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of 1000 that were seized with it, I believe scarcely one died; ... about the 2d day of the distemper, the patient usually of himself fell into a sweat, unless it was prevented by letting blood, which, however beneficial in other fevers, manifestly retarded the progress of this; and if the sweat was encouraged for 5 or 6 hours, by laying on more clothes, or taking some sudorific medicine, most of the complaints would entirely disappear, or at least very much abate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therapeutic criterion: for this transient epidemic cold, allow/encourage natural sweating (promote with coverings or sudorifics) and avoid bloodletting which delays recovery. Support recovery with fresh open air if symptoms persist. Duration and prognosis: usually resolves in days to weeks and rarely fatal except in already weakened individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epidemic observation and spatio-temporal pattern reporting (east-to-west progression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whence we may reasonably infer, that these spreading epidemic distempers take their progress from east to west.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When documenting epidemic spread, compare onset timing across locations (e.g., London vs Dublin) to infer directionality. Record dates of first appearance, peak prevalence, and abatement in different regions to support hypotheses about progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical/surgical refutations about urinary/bladder stone treatment in women
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr Molineux ... thinks that women never breed stones so large as men; the contrary of which seems to be manifest ... He seems to conclude it probable that all women may be freed from the stone by dilatation of the urinary passage ... which method I think cannot be depended on, since the stones may prove of so great a size. He says, that dividing the membranous substance of the bladder, is to be avoided as certain death to the patient: whereas this stone ... The patient never had the least ill symptom since her being cut, and is now perfectly well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clinical practice criteria derived from case evidence: (1) Women can form bladder stones as large as those in men; (2) simple dilatation of the urinary passage is not a reliable method for removing very large stones; (3) surgical incision within the short neck of a woman's bladder can be successful and is not invariably fatal. Use actual surgical outcomes to challenge prevailing beliefs and inform treatment choices.
